newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. officials question Rwanda tribunal officers.
newsitem.headline: U.N. officials question Rwanda tribunal officers.

text.p: Canadian Louise Arbour, the prosecutor for U.N. war crimes tribunals, said on Friday she feared that deteriorating security in Rwanda would hinder future investigations of the 1994 genocide.

Arbour, based in The Hague, was summoned to New York by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan along with other court officials as a result of a scathing U.N. report accusing the Rwanda tribunal of mismanagement and legal chaos.

U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said Annan would make changes but not announce them immediately. Arbour, who took up her post in October, said she had given him recommendations but that the violence in Rwanda had added another dimension to problems facing the court.

Arbour, who is also chief prosecutor for the tribunal on war crimes in the former Yugoslavia, said a security team would be sent to Rwanda immediately to make recommendations following the return of thousands of Hutu refugees from Zaire and subsequent increasing violence.
"It creates enormous concerns in our office in respect to the security of our witnesses to whom we no longer have the free access that we had before the return of the refugees," she told reporters.
"The opportunities that were there from September 1995 when the first investigators arrived are no longer there."
She also said "investigations have suffered a setback by administrative deprivation or inadequacies."

The court, based in Arusha, Tanzania, with a prosecutorial branch in Rwanda, was created more than two years ago to try key figures responsible for the 1994 genocide of more than 500,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Annan met Arbour as well as the court's registrar, Andronico Adede of Kenya based in Arusha and deputy prosecutor Honoure Rakotomanana of Madagascar, who is based in the Rwandan capital Kigali.

A report released last week by Karl Paschke, the U.N. equivalent of an inspector-general, said the court was riddled with administrative mismanagement, unqualified staff including its lawyers, and financial waste. He criticised the Kigali deputy prosecutor and the Arusha registrar's office.

The group also spoke to Hans Corell, the head of the legal affairs department, and Joseph Connor, head of the administration and management department, both of whom were criticised in the report for not providing more support.

Eckhard said that in addition to sending a security team, Connor had sent 105 personnel to the Rwanda tribunal "since the problem was first detected." He said key administrative positions were covered, at least temporarily.

Arbour, in answer to questions, said Corell's legal department took the view that tribunals were independent and that it was inappropriate to interfere. But she said "you can interfere, in a sense, by neglect".

The crisis within the Rwanda tribunal is becoming a major test for Annan, a 58-year old Ghanaian who began his term on Jan. 1. Some have urged Annan to fire anyone responsible for mismanaging the court's operations while others say the tribunal has received far less support than The Hague-based tribunal on the former Yugoslavia.
A total of 21 suspects have been indicted by the tribunal and Arbour said the court trials, which have been delayed considerably to date, would continue.
